title: Dynamic batch-shape probe: INT8 vs FP8 proxy performance and kernel handoff
body:
Context and motivation:
- Quick internal probe to understand how dynamic request shapes (variable sequence length + per-request batch size) change the runtime behavior between two quant strategies: hardware-backed INT8 kernels (our fused int8 kernels) and an FP8-proxy technique (simulated fp8 via blocked mixed-precision to emulate fp8 memory footprint while using fp16 compute).
- Goal: find common failure modes where INT8 throughput wins but quality regresses vs fp8-proxy, or where kernel handoff (dispatcher routing to fallback fast kernel) causes latency tail spikes at p95/p99.

Experiment summary (what we ran):
- Models: LLaMA-2-13B (dense transformer), small-run MPT-7B for sanity checks.
- Quantization methods tested: GPTQ-8bit baseline (post-GPTQ per-layer), our AWQ pipeline (recommended config), and FP8-proxy (blocked 8-bit storage with cast to fp16 for compute).
- Kernels: fused-attn-int8 (custom CUDA kernels), attention-cublas (fallback path using GEMM + cuBLAS), triton-block-kernel (in-dev), and cpu-fallback.
- Workloads: three synthetic traffic shapes created from prod traces (June 2026):
  * steady-small: batch sizes 1-4, seq_len 32-96 (most common, 68% of requests)
  * spiky-long: batch sizes 8-16, seq_len 256-1024 (rare but high cost)
  * mixed-mix: randomized batch 1-12, seq 16-512 with hot prefixes to exercise KV cache reuse
- Metrics: token/sec (throughput), p50/p95/p99 latency (ms per request forward), peak GPU memory (MB), model quality: avg logprob delta vs float16 baseline on a 500-sample held-out eval set (open-qa + doc-summarization mix), and a small human eval note column.

Key observations (raw):
1) steady-small workload:
   - fused-attn-int8: best token/sec at batch 1-4, p50 low (6-8ms), p95 acceptable (14-18ms). Memory reduced ~22% vs fp16. Quality: logprob delta +0.12 on average (small degradation, acceptable for many throughput-first customers).
   - fp8-proxy: slightly lower token/sec (~8% less) due to extra cast/pack/unpack overhead, p95 similar but p99 improved by ~10% (fewer micro-tail events). Quality delta +0.03 (near parity).
   - Notes: int8 shows more variability on requests with short prompt prefixes that cause many small GEMMs; kernel launch overhead and small-warp utilization are visible in perf traces.

2) spiky-long workload:
   - fused-attn-int8: throughput advantage disappears at seq_len >=512; p95/p99 explode when dispatcher tries to coalesce requests into a big batch but kernel memory allocator hits fragmentation and triggers fallback to attention-cublas for large heads. Observed p99 latencies >1200ms on peak.
   - fp8-proxy: holding memory density allowed more consistent batching; cast overhead amortized over long sequences, so token/sec > int8 in these shapes. Quality remained closer to fp16.
   - Observed allocator logs show repeated small CUDA malloc/free cycles during big-batch handling for INT8 code path; suspect our per-request allocator arena strategy fails under large-seq coalescing.

3) mixed-mix workload (KV cache heavy):
   - Both int8 and fp8-proxy benefited from KV cache reuse, but int8's tile-based KV packing introduced a small correctness flakiness in a ~2% subset of cases (manifested as mismatched past-key ordering when caching across variable-length prompts). We suspect an indexing bug in the packing routine under dynamic shapes.
   - Kernel handoff events (fast kernel -> fallback) are correlated with sequence length thresholds: when a request crosses a length threshold at runtime the dispatcher sometimes tries an incompatible packed-kv kernel and then emits a handoff. Each handoff costs ~20-30ms overhead plus extra memory churn.

Profiling hotspots (flamegraph notes):
- Top lines (int8 path): attention_fused_kernel (35% of runtime), kv_pack_unroll (12%), device_mem_align (8%), dispatcher_route (6%), softmax_int8_requantize (5%).
- Top lines (fp8-proxy path): cast_pack_unpack (20%), attention_fp16_kernel (40%), kv_store_write (10%), dispatcher_route (4%).
- Interesting: fp8-proxy spends more time in cast/pack but less in allocator churn; int8 spends more time in micro-memory ops and quant-specific requantize kernels.

Quality vs performance tradeoffs (numbers from the 500-sample eval):
- Metric: avg logprob delta (higher = worse compared to fp16 baseline), exact match (EM) for QA, rouge-L for summarization.
  * fused-int8 (GPTQ tuned): logprob delta +0.11, QA EM drop 3.7%, Rouge-L -1.8 points.
  * AWQ (our tuned per-channel config): logprob delta +0.06, QA EM drop 1.9%, Rouge-L -0.8 points.
  * FP8-proxy: logprob delta +0.02, QA EM drop 0.6%, Rouge-L -0.2 points.
- Operational takeaway: AWQ narrows quality gap while retaining much of int8 throughput; FP8-proxy is closest to fp16 quality but without the full runtime optimizations yet.

Failure cases and anomalies (notes-to-self):
- Memory allocator fragmentation under spiky-long workloads appears to be the largest operational risk for the int8 path. Reproduction steps in local: run mixed load generator with 60% spiky-long and inspect /proc/driver/nvidia/gpus/*/memory and runtime allocator logs.
- KV packing index mis-ordering under mixed-mix workload — add deterministic test that exercises variable-length KV caching and compare stored vs recomputed ordering. Suspect off-by-one in stride calculation when batch_size%tile != 0.
- Dispatcher threshold decisions: our current heuristics (seq_len thresholds at 128/256/512) are static. With dynamic workloads, a better cost model that uses current GPU memory pressure + estimated batch coalescing benefit would avoid unnecessary handoffs.

Small reproducer (commands):
- generator: python tools/loadgen.py --model llama-13b --quant awq --trace samples/june_prod_trace.json --clients 64 --shape-mix mixed-mix --duration 180
- profiler: CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1 python tools/trace_capture.py --pid <runtime_pid> --output /tmp/trace.json --duration 60
- quick diff quality: python eval/run_logprob_diff.py --base fp16_baseline.tok --cand quant_run.tok --output quick-diff.csv

Immediate recommendations (short):
1) Patch allocator: convert arena to per-thread arenas with a bump-pointer fallback for large contiguous allocations to reduce fragmentation during large-seq coalescing. High priority.
2) Add a pre-dispatch cost model: lightweight estimator that predicts whether coalescing into a large batch will exceed allocator headroom and chooses to schedule smaller batches or use fp16 fallback. Medium priority.
3) KV packing unit-tests and fixed-indexing check. Medium-high priority.
4) AWQ should be promoted as the default for hosted low-latency tiers; int8-fused for dedicated high-throughput where customers accept small quality delta. Low-latency hosted should default to fp8-proxy once we optimize cast overhead.

Open questions and experiments to run next:
- Can we push a single pass kernel that fuses cast/unpack for fp8-proxy to recover the ~8% token/sec gap? Prototype with Triton kernel.
- What is the break-even point (seq_len x batch) where int8 wins again? Need a 2D sweep and heatmap.
- Investigate CUDA MemPool (memcached) vs our custom arena under mixed loads — does MemPool reduce fragmentation?

Human eval notes (quick):
- 10 sampled summaries from spiky-long: fp8-proxy and AWQ outputs are indistinguishable in readability; fused-int8 had 2 cases with hallucinated entity.

Next steps and owners:
- Marco: allocator prototyping and benchmark (due 2026-07-30).
- Priya: KV packing unit-tests and deterministic reproducer (due 2026-07-25).
- Anika (me): prototype triton fused-cast kernel for fp8-proxy and run 2D sweep (seq_len x batch) by 2026-08-05.

Notes to self / scratchpad (raw):
- observed many 'handoff' log lines around 2026-07-05 14:02:12 UTC when spike generator ran — attach full log to JIRA-RT-1147.
- perf counters: SM utilization dips to 35% on int8 for seq_len 64 small batches; need to see serialized kernel launches.

References and links inside org:
- design doc: confluence.redwood/serving/runtime/quantization-proposal (draft)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/812 (allocator changes, WIP)
- JIRA: JIRA-RT-1147 (KV packing bug)

Conclusion (one-liner):
- No single quant strategy is best across highly dynamic production shapes — INT8 yields peak throughput but is brittle under large-seq spikes and allocator pressure; AWQ is a pragmatic middle ground; FP8-proxy gives the best quality envelope and must be optimized in kernel packing to be competitive on raw token/sec.

End of note.
